source_text: 1. Quia ergo post primas illas dissertiones, quas de patre et filio et spiritu sancto in initiis seeundum quod res poposcerat exposuimus, visum est rursum repetere nos debere et ostendere quod deus idem esset creator et conditor mundi et pater domini nostri lesu Christi, id est legis et prophetarum atque evangeliorum unus atque idem deus, tum deinde etiam de Christo, quod is, qui verbum et sapientia dei superius fuerat ostensus, etiam qualiter homo factus est in consequentibus debuit demonstrari: superest ut etiam de spiritu sancto quam possumus breviter repetamus. j Tempus est ergo nunc de spiritu saneto nos pro viribus pauca disserere, quem dominus et salvator noster in evangelio secundum lohannem ‘paracletum’ nominavit. Sicut enim idem ipse deus atque idem ipse Christus, ita idem ipse et spiritus sanctus est, qui et in prophetis et in apostolis fuit, id est sive in illis, qui ante adventum Christi deo crediderunt, sive in his, qui per Christum confugerunt ad deum. Et duos quidem deos ausos esse haereticos dicere et duos Christos audivimus, duos autem spiritus sanctos numquam cognovimus ab aliquo praedicari. Quomodo enim hoc de scripturis poterunt affirmare, aut quam differentiam dare poterunt inter spiritum sanctum et spiritum sanctum? si tamen definitio aliqua aut descriptio inveniri potest spiritus saneti. Nam ut concedamus Marcioni vel Valentino posse differentias deitatis inducere et aliam boni naturam aliam vero 1usti describere, quid excogitabit aut quid inveniet, ut differentiam sancti spiritus introdueat? Nihil ergo illos posse ad indicium qualiscumque differentiae arbitror invenire. 2. Nos vero aestimamus quod participationem eius similiter ut sapientiae dei et verbi dei absque ulla differentia creatura rationabilis omnis assumat. Video tamen quod praecipuus spiritus sancti adventus ad homines post ascensionem Christi in caelos magis quam ante adventum elus declaretur. Antea namque solis prophetis et paucis, si qui forte in populo meruisset, donum sancti spiritus praebebatur; post adventum vero salvatoris scriptum est ‘adimpletum esse illud, quod dietum fuerat in propheta lohele quia “erit in novissimis diebus, et effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem, et prophetabunt”; quod utique tale est sicut illud, quod ait: “Omnes gentes servient eic. Per : gratiam ergo saneti spiritus cum reliquis quam plurimis etiam illud magnificentissimum demonstratur, quod ea, quae in prophetis seripta sunt vel in lege Moysi, pauci tune. x, id est ipsi prophetae et vix sicubi unus ex omni populo superare poterat intellectum corporeum et maius aliquid. sentire, id est spiritale quid poterat intellegere in lege vel prophetis; nune autem innumerae sunt multitudines credentium, qui lice& non omnes possint per ordinem atque ad liquidum spiritalis intellegentiae explanare consequentiam, tamen omnes paene persuasum habent quod neque circumcisio corporaliter intellegi debeat neque otium sabbati vel sanguinis effusio pecoris, neque quod de his Moysi responsa darentur a deo: qui utique sensus dubium non est quod spiritus sancti virtute omnibus suggeratur. 3. Sicut. autem multi sunt intellectus de Christo, qui utique quamvis "saplentia- sit, non tamen in omnibus sapientiae agit aut obtinet vim nisi in his, qui in ipso sapientiae student (neque cum -medicus- dicatur, erga omnes quasi medicus agit, sed erga illos tantum, qui aegritudinis suae intellecto languore confugiunt ad misericordiam eius, ut possint consequi sanitatem): ita arbitror etiam de spiritu sancto, in quo omnis est natura donorum. ‘Aliis’ namque praebetur ‘per spiritum sermo sapientiae, alüs sermo scientiae, alüs fides’; et ita per singulos, qui eum capere possunt, hoc efficitur vel hoc intellegitur ipse spiritus, quo indiget ille, qui eum participare meruerit. Quas divisiones ac differentias non advertentes hi, qui “paracletum- eum in evangelio audiunt nominari, neque considerantes ex quo opere vel actu “paracletusnominetur, vilbus eum nescio quibus spiritibus compararunt et per hoe conturbare conati sunt ecclesias Christi, ita ut dissensiones fratribus non modicas generarent. Evangelium vero tantae eum potentiae ac maiestatis ostendit, ut dicat apostolos ‘non posse capere- adhue ea, quae volebat eos docere salvator, nisi -cum advenerit spiritus sanctus’, qui se eorum animabus infundens inluminare eos possit de ratione ac fide trinitatis. Isti vero pro imperitia intellectus sui, qua non solum ipsi quod rectum est consequenter non valent exponere, sed ne his quidem quae a nobis dicuntur possunt audientiam commodare, minora de eius deitate quam dignum est sentientes, erroribus se ac deceptionibus tradiderunt, erratico magis spiritu depravati quam sancti spiritus institutionibus eruditi, secundum quod apostolus dixit: “Doctrinam spirituum daemoniorum sequentes, prohibentium nubere” “ad interitum et ruinam multorum” “et inportune se abstinere a cibis”, ut per ostentationem acrioris observantiae seducant animas innocentum, 4. Oportet ergo nos scire quia ‘paracletus’ est spiritus sanctus, docens maiora quam voce proferri possunt et, ut ita dixerim, quae ‘ineffabilia sunt- et “quae non licet homini loqui”, id est quae indicari humano sermone non possunt. Quod autem ait “non licet”, pro eo quod ‘non potest- dietum sentimus a Paulo, sicut et ibi, ubi ait: “Omnia lieent, sed non omnia expediunt; omnia licent, sed non omnia aedifieant”, Ea enim, quorum potestas nobis est, propter quod habere ea possumus, -licere- nobis dicit. ‘Paracletus’ vero quod dicitur spiritus sanctus, a consolatione dieitur enim latine consolatio appellatur); si quis namque de spiritu sancto participare meruerit, cognitis ineffabilibus sacramentis consolationem sine dubio et laetitiam cordis assumit. Cum enim rationes omnium quae fiunt, quare vel qualiter fiant, spiritu indicante cognoverit, in nullo utique conturbari eius anima poterit aut ullum sensum maeroris accipere; nec in aliquo terretur, cum verbo dei et sapientiae eius inhaerens ‘dominum lesum dicit in spiritu sancto-. Verum quoniam ‘paracleti- fecimus mentionem et pro viribus nostris qualiter de eo sentiri debeat exposuimus, dicitur autem etiam salvator noster ‘paracletus’ in epistola lohannis, cum dicit: “5i quis nostrum peccaverit, paracletum habemus ad patrem, lesum Christum iustum, et ipse est repropitiatio pro peccatis nostris”: consideremus ne forte aliud hie significet haec appellatio “paracleti- de salvatore, aliud de spiritu saneto. Videtur enim de salvatore ‘paracletus’ dici depreeator, utrumque enim significat in graeco ‘paracletus’, et “consolatoret “deprecator. Propter eum ergo qui subsequitur sermonem, quo ait quia “ipse est repropitiatio pro peccatis nostris”, magis in salvatore nomen “paraeleti- pro deprecatore intellegendum videtur; deprecari enim patrem ‘pro peccatis nostris. dicitur. De spiritu vero sancto “paracletus’ ‘consolator’ debet intellegi, pro eo quod consolationem praestat animabus, quibus aperit et revelat sensum scientiae spiritalis.

pass_b_english: Because we have already laid out our first discussions on the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as the subject demanded, we now consider it necessary to go back and show that God is the same Creator and Founder of the world and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, one and the same God of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels—and then also to demonstrate about Christ that the one who was shown above to be the Word and Wisdom of God should also be shown in what follows to have become man. It remains, therefore, for us to speak briefly about the Holy Spirit as well, as far as we are able. (John 14:16) Now is the time for us to discuss a few things about the Holy Spirit according to our strength, whom our Lord and Savior named "Paraclete" in the Gospel according to John. For just as it is the same God and the same Christ, so also it is the same Holy Spirit who was in the prophets and in the apostles—that is, either in those who believed in God before Christ's coming, or in those who through Christ took refuge in God. We have heard that some heretics dared to say there are two gods and two Christs, but we have never known anyone to preach two Holy Spirits. For how could they affirm this from the Scriptures, or what difference could they give between the Holy Spirit and the Holy Spirit, if indeed any definition or description of the Holy Spirit can be found? Even if we grant Marcion or Valentinus the power to introduce differences in divinity and to describe one nature as good and another as just, what will they devise or find to introduce a difference in the Holy Spirit? I think, therefore, that they can find nothing to indicate any kind of difference.

We, however, judge that every rational creature similarly assumes a participation in the Holy Spirit, just as in the Wisdom of God and the Word of God, without any difference. I see, however, that the chief coming of the Holy Spirit to human beings is declared more after the ascension of Christ into heaven than before his coming. For previously the gift of the Holy Spirit was given only to the prophets and to a few, if any in the people had deserved it; but after the coming of the Savior it is written, "And it shall be in the last days, says God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy" (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17); and this is just like that which says, "All nations shall serve him." Therefore, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, along with many others, that most magnificent fact is also demonstrated: those things which were written in the prophets or in the Law of Moses, few at that time—that is, the prophets themselves and scarcely any one person from the whole people—were able to surpass bodily understanding and to perceive something greater, that is, to understand something spiritual in the Law or the Prophets. But now there are innumerable multitudes of believers who, although not all can explain the sequence of spiritual understanding in order and clearly, nevertheless almost all have the conviction that circumcision should not be understood bodily, nor the rest of the Sabbath, nor the pouring out of the blood of cattle, nor that the responses about these things were given by God through Moses—which sense is undoubtedly suggested to all by the power of the Holy Spirit.

But just as there are many understandings of Christ, which, although it is Wisdom, nevertheless does not act or obtain force in all except in those who strive for Wisdom in it (for just as when he is called "Physician," he does not act as a physician toward all, but only toward those who, recognizing the languor of their sickness, flee to his mercy so that they may obtain health), so I think also about the Holy Spirit, in whom is the whole nature of gifts. "To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another faith" (1 Cor 12:8-9); and thus through each one who is able to receive him, this or that is effected or understood—this Spirit, which he needs who has deserved to participate in him. Those who hear the "Paraclete" named in the Gospel, not noticing these divisions and differences, and not considering from what work or act the "Paraclete" is named, have compared him to I know not what spirits and have attempted to disturb the churches of Christ through this, so that they generated not small dissensions among brothers. The Gospel, however, shows him of such great power and majesty, that it says the apostles "could not yet bear those things which the Savior wanted to teach them, unless the Holy Spirit should come" (John 16:12), who, pouring himself into their souls, might illuminate them concerning the reason and faith of the Trinity. But these men, because of the unskillfulness of their own understanding—by which they are not only unable to explain what is right consequentially, but cannot even give a hearing to what we say—feeling less about his divinity than is worthy, have handed themselves over to errors and deceptions, corrupted by an erratic spirit rather than instructed by the teachings of the Holy Spirit, according to what the Apostle said: "Following the teachings of the spirits of demons, forbidding to marry... to destruction and ruin of many... and inappropriately abstaining from foods" (1 Tim 4:1-3), so that through the display of a sharper observance they might seduce innocent souls.

Therefore it is necessary for us to know that "Paraclete" is the Holy Spirit, teaching things greater than can be uttered by voice, and, so to speak, things "which are unspeakable and which it is not permitted for a human to speak" (2 Cor 12:4)—that is, things which cannot be indicated by human speech. But what he says, "it is not permitted," we understand as said for "it is not possible" by Paul, just as also there where he says: "All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient; all things are lawful, but not all things edify" (1 Cor 10:23). For those things whose power is ours, because of which we are able to have them, he says are "lawful" for us. But the Holy Spirit is called "Paraclete" from consolation (for in Latin consolation is called consolatio); for if anyone deserves to participate in the Holy Spirit, having come to know the unspeakable sacraments, he undoubtedly assumes consolation and joy of heart. For when, the Spirit indicating, he has come to know the reasons of all things that happen—why or how they happen—his soul will certainly not be able to be disturbed in anything nor receive any sense of sorrow; nor is he terrified in anything, clinging to the Word of God and his Wisdom, saying "Jesus is Lord in the Holy Spirit" (1 Cor 12:3). But since we have made mention of the "Paraclete" and have explained as far as our strength allows how one ought to feel about him, our Savior is also called "Paraclete" in the Epistle of John, when he says: "If anyone of us has sinned, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 2:1-2). Let us consider whether this title "Paraclete" might perhaps signify one thing concerning the Savior, another concerning the Holy Spirit. For "Paraclete" seems to be said of the Savior as "Advocate," for both are signified in Greek by "Paraclete": both "Comforter" and "Advocate." Because of him who follows in the discourse, where he says "and he is the propitiation for our sins," the name "Paraclete" in the Savior seems more to be understood as "Advocate"; for he is said to intercede with the Father "for our sins." But of the Holy Spirit "Paraclete" must be understood as "Comforter," because he provides consolation to souls, to whom he opens and reveals the sense of spiritual knowledge.
